terms.definition: The set of protein polymers inside a cell that give it shape, hold its parts in place, anchor it to its neighbours and to the material beneath it, and generate movement. Three systems make it up in an animal cell: actin filaments, microtubules and intermediate filaments. The name suggests a rigid frame, and that part of the everyday sense is misleading; these polymers are assembled, disassembled and rebuilt continuously while the cell is working.

A thin, polar polymer of actin subunits, about 7 nanometres across, with a persistence length of 3 to 17 micrometres so that a single filament is rod-like over about a micrometre and floppy over the height of a cell. Subunits are added preferentially at its barbed or plus end, and myosin motors move along it, so an actin structure can both hold a shape and be pulled on under the cell's control. Cross-linking many filaments into a bundle makes the assembly far stiffer than any one filament.

A hollow, polar polymer of tubulin about 25 nanometres in outside diameter, and by a wide margin the stiffest of the three filament systems: its persistence length exceeds a millimetre, which is more than forty times the height of an absorptive intestinal cell, so one microtubule crossing such a cell is effectively a straight rod. Kinesins and dyneins move along it, which makes it suited to defining an axis and running directed traffic along that axis.

A rope-like cytoskeletal polymer, apolar because its dimers associate in an anti-parallel fashion into tetramers with no net direction. It is the floppiest of the three systems as a single filament, with a persistence length of a few hundred nanometres to about a micrometre, and the toughest under stretch, extending beyond 200 per cent of its resting length without breaking and stiffening as it is strained further. Because it is apolar it carries no molecular motors, so nothing travels along one in a chosen direction.

The intermediate filament protein family of epithelial cells, and so the polymer an epithelial desmosome anchors. In this lesson keratin is the tension-bearing member of the cytoskeleton: it is what desmoplakin grips, and its mechanical properties are the intermediate filament properties described above.

The property of a cytoskeletal polymer whose two ends differ, so that subunits are added preferentially at one of them and motor proteins can tell one end from the other. Actin filaments and microtubules have it; intermediate filaments do not. This is a different sense of the word from the cell polarity earlier lessons in this block used, where a polarised cell is one with distinct apical and basolateral surfaces. A cell can be polarised in that sense while containing filaments that are themselves apolar.

The distance along a filament over which it stays roughly straight against the random thermal motion of the surrounding water. Below that distance the filament behaves as a rod; well above it, the filament bends appreciably. It is the single number this lesson uses to compare filament stiffness, and it is only informative once divided by the length of the structure that has to be held.

A protein that spends chemical energy to move along a polar cytoskeletal filament in a particular direction, carrying a load or generating force. Myosins move on actin filaments; kinesins and dyneins move on microtubules. A motor requires a filament whose ends differ, which is why intermediate filaments have none.

One finger-like projection of an absorptive cell's apical surface, about a micrometre long and about a hundred nanometres across, held out against the surface tension of a fluid membrane by a core bundle of roughly 19 cross-linked actin filaments and guyed to that membrane by myosin cross-bridges. The plural is microvilli. A microvillus is a single projection and is not the array: the array is the brush border, and the two words are not interchangeable.

alignment.note: PREM-BIO-004 glosses microvillus inside its brush border entry, as one projection of the array, and states that the two words are not interchangeable. This lesson keeps that distinction exactly and promotes the single projection to its own term, because the projection's actin core is this lesson's subject. The array sense stays with the earlier lesson's brush border entry; microvillus is not an alias of it. Readers should note that PREM-BIO-003 and PREM-BIO-004 give brush border slightly different definitions, and this lesson follows PREM-BIO-004's figures.

terms.definition: The layer of cross-linked filaments just beneath the bases of the microvillar core bundles, containing a non-erythrocytic spectrin that ties adjacent bundles to one another as they enter the apical cytoplasm. It is the mat the microvillar rods are planted in, and it is also where keratin anchored at the desmosomes reaches, which makes the apical and lateral cytoskeletons mechanically continuous.

The set of attachment structures joining one epithelial cell to its neighbours, arranged in a fixed order from the apical surface downward: tight junction, then adherens junction, then desmosomes. The word complex invites the assumption that they work as one machine, and this lesson's evidence is that they do not: each grips its own cytoskeletal polymer and each fails separately.

The most apical of the cell-to-cell attachments, and the only one that seals the space between neighbouring cells: at it the intercellular space disappears, and it is the rate-limiting step for movement between cells instead of through them. Built from claudins, occludin and JAM-A, with ZO-1, ZO-2 and ZO-3 scaffolds tying them to actin. Its claudins form charge-selective pores, so it is a regulated gate rather than a plug.

alignment.note: PREM-BIO-004 established the tight junction as a fence acting in the outer leaflet of the membrane only, which keeps the apical and basolateral surfaces of one cell different. That sense is adopted here unchanged and is restated in scene 4. This lesson extends it by adding the protein composition and the second, separate job of sealing the route between two cells. The two jobs act at right angles to each other, and neither replaces the other.

terms.definition: The attachment below the tight junction, built from the transmembrane proteins E-cadherin and nectin with cytoplasmic catenins connected directly to actin, and associated with a belt of actin around the cell. It starts and stabilises contact between neighbouring cells. It holds cells together without sealing the space between them; at an adherens junction the neighbouring membranes stay 15 to 20 nanometres apart.

The attachment below the adherens junction, and the one that does not use actin. Desmosomal cadherins, the desmogleins and desmocollins, reach across to the neighbouring cell; plakoglobin and the plakophilins sit on the cytoplasmic face; and desmoplakin anchors keratin intermediate filaments to the membrane. Its job is mechanical coupling under load, which is why it is wired to the polymer that holds force at higher tensile loads than actin. Like the adherens junction, it adheres without sealing.

A transmembrane receptor, made of an alpha and a beta subunit, by which a cell binds the matrix outside it. In the human intestinal crypt integrins bind the laminins and fibronectin of the basement membrane, and integrin-linked kinase provides a physical link from the integrin beta1 tail to actin. So the attachment facing downward is an actin-linked one, like two of the three that face sideways.

The sheet of extracellular material an epithelium sits on, containing laminins, fibronectin, collagen and other matrix components, which the cells above it grip through integrins. Despite the name it is not a lipid bilayer and is not a membrane in the sense this block has used that word so far; it is secreted matrix, and it lies outside the cell rather than enclosing it.

alignment.note: PREM-BIO-004 names the basement membrane inside its basolateral membrane entry, as what the basolateral face looks onto beneath the sheet, without defining it. This lesson gives it its own bounded sense because the basal attachment is part of this outcome. Nothing in the earlier usage is changed. The note that it is not a bilayer is included deliberately, because PREM-BIO-004 owns membrane in the strict two-lipid-molecule sense and the same word is doing a different job in this compound.

terms.definition: Movement of cells that stay attached to one another throughout, so that a cell's direction is set by its neighbours and by the force transmitted between them, rather than chosen independently. Cells leaving a crypt move this way: velocity aligns with the traction the sheet exerts on the matrix, and cells further along drag those behind. It differs from a single cell crawling in culture, which has a free front edge and can make and break adhesions at will.
